summary: Defines the standard profile for Route Origin Authorizations (ROAs). A ROA is a digitally signed object showing that an IP address block holder has authorized an Autonomous System to originate routes to prefixes in that block. It obsoletes RFC 6482.

eli5.summary: A ROA is a signed permission slip saying which network is allowed to announce a set of internet addresses, to stop impostors.

questions: what does maxlength mean in a roa
subtitle: The signed permission slip that says which AS may originate routes for an address block, and how it is encoded.

tldr.problem: Routing needs a way to check that an Autonomous System has been given permission by the holder of an IP address block to advertise routes to prefixes in that block.
tldr.mechanism: A ROA is an RPKI signed object, wrapped in CMS, that names one AS number and a list of IPv4 and IPv6 prefixes, each with an optional maxLength. Relying Parties validate it against the signing certificate's address resources.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9582 obsoletes RFC 6482. It tightens the ASN.1, adds a canonical ordering for the prefix list, and clarifies the certificate extensions.

facts.label: Address families
facts.value: IPv4 (0001) and IPv6 (0002), at most one group each

today: RFC 9582 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2024. It obsoletes RFC 6482 and is not itself obsoleted or updated by any RFC listed in the metadata.

sections.title: Introduction and Changes
sections.content:
The main purpose of the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) is to improve routing security. As part of it, a mechanism is needed to verify that an Autonomous System (AS) has been given permission by an address block holder to advertise routes to prefixes in that block. A Route Origin Authorization (ROA) provides this.

A ROA reuses the RPKI signed object template (RFC 6488), which wraps content in a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) envelope. This document therefore only defines the identifying OID, the ASN.1 syntax of the payload (encoded with DER), and the extra validation steps.

It obsoletes RFC 6482. Changes: clearer rules for the IP address and AS identifier certificate extensions, stronger ASN.1, errata incorporated, an example ROA, and a canonicalization procedure for ipAddrBlocks.
sections.eli5: A ROA is like a note from the owner of a house saying which delivery company may drop parcels there. It is signed so nobody can fake it.

sections.title: What a ROA Contains
sections.content:
The content type is id-ct-routeOriginAuthz, with the numerical value 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.24. It MUST appear both as the eContentType and as the content-type signed attribute.

The payload, RouteOriginAttestation, has three parts. The version MUST be 0. The asID is the single AS number being authorized. The ipAddrBlocks are the prefixes it may originate. If a holder wants to authorize several ASes for the same prefixes, it issues one ROA per AS number.

Prefixes are grouped by address family, using AFI 0001 for IPv4 and 0002 for IPv6. There MUST be only one group per AFI, so at most two. IPv4 prefixes MUST NOT appear as IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses. Each prefix is a ROAIPAddress with an address bit string and an optional maxLength. ROAs represent only prefixes, which is more restrictive than the arbitrary ranges the RFC 3779 extension can carry.
sections.eli5: The slip names one company and lists the street addresses it may deliver to. If you want to allow two companies, you write two slips.

sections.title: The maxLength Element
sections.content:
When present, maxLength is the longest (most specific) prefix length the AS may advertise within the listed prefix. It MUST be at least the prefix length and at most 32 for IPv4 or 128 for IPv6. When it is absent, the AS may advertise only the exact prefix.

The RFC's example is the prefix 203.0.113.0/24 with maxLength 26. The AS may advertise 203.0.113.0/24, 203.0.113.128/25 or 203.0.113.192/26, but not 203.0.113.0/27.

The element SHOULD NOT be encoded when it equals the prefix length, and Certification Authorities should expect future Relying Parties to treat superfluous maxLength values as encoding errors. The RFC points to RFC 9319 for guidance on using maxLength. A ROA may contain a prefix covered by another prefix in the same ROA, but listing the identical prefix twice is NOT RECOMMENDED, because the one with the shorter maxLength adds nothing.
sections.eli5: maxLength says how small a piece of your address block the company may announce. Without it, they may only announce the whole block.

sections.title: Canonical Form for the Prefix List
sections.content:
The syntax allows many ways to write the same set of prefixes. To give each set one unique representation, the RFC defines a canonical form that SHOULD be used, with entries unique and sorted ascending. Certification Authorities should expect future Relying Parties to require it strictly.

Each entry is mapped to four integers: afi, addr (the first address as an integer), plen (prefix length) and mlen (the maxLength, or the prefix length if absent). Entries are ordered by afi, then addr, then plen, then mlen, each lower value first. Entries equal in all four are duplicates. The RFC lists example sorting implementations in C and Rust.
sections.eli5: It is a rule for putting the list in the same order every time, like sorting a class by name, so two people writing the same list produce identical results.

sections.title: Validating a ROA
sections.content:
A Relying Party MUST validate a ROA before using it, performing all checks in RFC 6488 plus ROA-specific ones on the end-entity (EE) certificate inside the ROA.

  • The IP address delegation extension is present, and every prefix in the payload lies within the addresses it lists.
  • That extension MUST NOT contain inherit elements.
  • The AS identifier delegation extension MUST NOT be present.
  • The content fully conforms to Sections 3 and 4.

If any check fails, the whole ROA MUST be considered invalid and an error SHOULD be logged.
sections.eli5: Before trusting a slip, you check that the person who signed it really owns every address on it. If even one address is not theirs, you throw the whole slip away.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A ROA is not confidential; it is expected to sit in repositories open to all ISPs and perhaps all Internet users. There is no explicit authentication, because the PKI provides authorization rather than authentication, and the ROA is not meant to convey non-repudiation.

What matters is integrity. The signer's right to authorize the AS comes from the address space and AS number PKI described in RFC 6480: one MUST verify the signature with a certificate issued under that PKI and check that the ROA prefixes lie within the certificate's IP address delegation extension. All security considerations of RFC 6488 and of CMS also apply.
sections.eli5: Anyone may read the slip. What matters is that nobody could have changed it and that the signer really owns the addresses.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA updated several registries to point to this RFC: the S/MIME CMS content type entry id-ct-routeOriginAuthz (decimal 24), the RPKI Signed Objects registry, the .roa file extension in the RPKI repository name schemes, and the media type application/rpki-roa. It also allocated module identifier 75, id-mod-rpkiROA-2023.

The RFC's appendix gives a DER example: asID 65536 with the single IPv6 prefix 2001:db8::/32, plus a complete Base64 encoded ROA object of 1668 octets.
sections.eli5: IANA is the librarian. It wrote down the ROA's name tag, file ending and type label in its catalogues.
